sessions.title: Awake at 3am
script: Shh… it's alright.
You're awake, in the middle of the night. That's okay.
You haven't done anything wrong. Sleep comes in waves, and sometimes you drift up to the surface between two of them.
It happens to almost everyone. Even the people who sleep like logs.
Don't reach for your phone. Don't check the time.
The number on the screen wouldn't tell you anything useful. It would only start the sums: how many hours are left, what time the alarm goes off.
Those sums can wait. There is no time right now. There's only the night.
If you're on your side, stay on your side. If you're on your back, stay on your back.
You don't need the perfect position. Just one that's good enough.
Adjust the pillow if you need to. Then let your head sink back into it, with all its weight.
Feel the pillow giving way a little under your cheek, under your temple. That's what it's there for.
[pause 3s]
Here's something true, and reassuring.
Lying still, eyes closed, in the quiet, is not wasted time.
Your body is already resting. Your muscles are softening. Your heart is slowing. Your breathing is settling.
Even awake, you're recovering. Not as much as in sleep, of course. But far more than you might think.
So for now, you don't have to sleep. You only have to rest.
And that, you know how to do. In fact, you're already doing it, right now, without any effort at all.
Nobody is grading you. There's no good night or bad night to hand in tomorrow morning. There's only this moment, lying here, in the quiet.
[pause 4s]
Maybe your mind woke up with you.
A conversation from yesterday. An email you need to send. A worry that grows bigger in the dark.
That's very common at night. Thoughts look larger, heavier, more urgent.
Not because they're more serious. Because it's dark, because you're tired, and a tired mind sees everything in deeper shades.
A bit like a shadow on the wall that looks huge because of where the lamp is.
Tomorrow morning, with a coffee and some daylight, the very same thought will be back to its normal size.
You can tell it, very gently: not now. We'll deal with this tomorrow.
The way you'd set something down on the nightstand, to pick it up when you wake.
It doesn't vanish. It simply waits for morning. That's where it belongs.
If it's something you mustn't forget, imagine writing it on a little yellow sticky note, stuck to the fridge door.
The note is there. It will remember for you. You don't have to hold on to it anymore.
If a thought comes back, that's fine. Set it down again. Not now. Tomorrow.
As many times as it takes. Without getting cross with it, or with yourself.
And each time you set it down, it gets a little easier. Like a small gesture your hands already know by heart.
[pause 4s]
Now, notice where you are.
The duvet, resting on you. Its light weight on your shoulders, your hips, your legs.
The warmth that gathered underneath while you were sleeping. Warmth that comes from you.
It wraps around your back, your belly, the tops of your thighs. A soft, even warmth that asks for nothing in return.
Feel your feet at the bottom of the bed. Maybe one patch of sheet is cooler, another warmer.
Your toes can uncurl. Your ankles can soften. Your calves grow a little heavier, sinking into the mattress.
Feel the softness of the fabric against your cheek, or the back of your neck.
Feel the mattress holding you. It asks nothing of you. It simply holds you.
Your hips sink in a little. Your back spreads out. All of your weight can settle there, with nothing held back.
Notice your hands, too. Under the pillow, on your belly, or by your sides.
Leave them where they are. They have nothing to carry tonight. No phone, no keys, no bag. Just the sheet.
Your fingers can open slightly. Your palms grow warm, heavy, and still.
You're sheltered. Outside, the night carries on without you. In here, it's warm and quiet.
There's nothing to keep watch over. Nobody needs you, right here, right now.
The house is asleep. The street is asleep. You can settle into this warmth, like a nest.
[pause 4s]
Your breath, now.
No need to change it much. Just let the out-breath stretch a little.
Like a very slow sigh that leaves on its own.
No numbers. No counting. Just a breath that goes out… a little more slowly than it came in.
The air comes in, without effort. And it leaves, taking its time.
Like a wave drawing back across the sand, in no hurry at all.
Then another wave rolls in. And it draws back, even more slowly than the last.
Each time the air goes out, something lets go a little. The shoulders. The jaw. The forehead.
The small space between your eyebrows. The hollows of your hands.
Your tongue can rest, soft, in the floor of your mouth. Your lips can part, just barely.
Your eyelids are heavy and warm. They rest over your eyes like a tiny blanket.
If your mind wanders back to the day, that's fine. Just come back to the air going out. Slowly.
And if your heart is beating a little fast, let it. It will slow down by itself, in time with this quiet breath.
If a breath ever feels uncomfortable, or too long, simply go back to breathing naturally. Your body knows how.
[pause 4s]
And now, a small surprising thing.
Instead of trying to sleep, you could try the opposite.
Staying awake. Peacefully. With your eyes closed.
Not by fighting. Not by forcing. Just by telling yourself: I'm staying awake, here, in the warm, and that's perfectly fine.
When you stop trying to sleep, the pressure drops. And often, without warning, sleep slips back in through the back door.
But that isn't the goal. The goal is simply to be here. Awake. At peace.
Keep your eyelids closed, heavy and soft.
You can even tell yourself: I'm keeping watch. Keeping watch over this quiet night.
Like a night guard with nothing to guard. Just sitting calmly while everything sleeps.
Listen to the night. The silence. Maybe the hum of the fridge. A car, very far away.
You stay awake… without doing anything with being awake.
No sounds to listen out for, no thoughts to sort through. Just being here, in the soft dark of the room, breathing.
If your eyelids grow heavy, you don't have to stop them. If they stay light, that's fine too.
If these night wakings happen often and weigh on your days, a health professional can help you make sense of them. But that's for tomorrow, too.
[pause 4s]
For now, there's only this.
The warmth. The breath. The night.
Your arms are heavy. Your legs are heavy.
Your head sinks a little deeper into the pillow.
Your face is smooth and still. Your belly rises, and falls.
Nothing to get right. Nothing to wait for.
The air comes in… and drifts away.
Again… and again… so gently.
Just staying here…
warm…
peaceful.

sessions.title: Close the day gently
script: Here you are, in bed. The day is behind you, or very nearly.
If the light is still on, you can switch it off now, or dim it to its softest.
Settle in the way you like to fall asleep. On your back, on your side, the duvet pulled up as far as you like.
Feel the weight of your head in the pillow. The mattress under your back, under your hips, under your heels.
For a few minutes, we'll close this day together. The way you close a book, slipping a bookmark between the pages.
Not to judge it. Not to replay every move. Just to put it away before you sleep.
There's nothing to get right here. If you fall asleep along the way, that's perfect too.
Begin with a few slow breaths.
Breathe in through your nose, unhurried. Feel the air gently filling your chest, then your belly.
And let the air flow out, even more slowly. Like a long end-of-the-day sigh.
Once more. Cool air coming in. Warm air going out.
One last time. And as you breathe out, let your shoulders sink back into the pillow.
Then let your breath find its own rhythm again. You don't need to look after it anymore.
[pause 4s]
Now you're going to rewind your day. Like a film playing backwards, on fast-forward.
No need to pause on every scene. The images roll by, and you watch them pass.
If your mind wants to linger somewhere, to analyse or comment, that's fine. You notice, and you let the film roll on.
You're not the judge of this day. Just the audience, sunk into a soft seat at the back of the cinema.
Start with right now. You, in this bed.
Just before: brushing your teeth. The bathroom light. Warm water running over your hands.
Before that: the evening. Dinner, maybe. A screen, a conversation, the clatter of dishes.
Coming home. The key in the lock. The bag dropped on the floor. Maybe kicking off your shoes, at last.
Late afternoon. The sky through the window, the light shifting.
The afternoon. Faces, voices, tasks. Some done, some not.
Lunch. What you ate, who you were with, or whether you were alone.
The morning. The commute. The first coffee. The first few minutes after waking.
And right at the start, waking itself. You, in this same bed, this morning.
The loop is closed. A whole day, from this morning all the way back to this pillow.
[pause 4s]
Maybe one scene in that film caught your eye. A hard moment.
Words that stung. Something that went wrong. Tiredness. A worry that wouldn't let go.
You don't need to live it again. You can simply acknowledge it. That was hard today.
Notice whether that memory has left a trace in your body. A weight on your chest, a tight throat, a knot in your stomach.
Rest a hand there, if you'd like. Just a warm hand, not trying to fix anything.
Feel the warmth of your palm seeping gently through the fabric. Let your breath move slowly beneath your hand.
You're allowed to find it hard. And you got through it. You're here, warm, tonight.
Now imagine picking up that moment and placing it in a box. A plain cardboard box.
You close the lid. You set it at the foot of the bed, or on a shelf, far from your pillow.
It will still be there tomorrow, if you need to deal with it. But not tonight.
If other difficult moments show up, they can go in the same box. There's room for all of them.
[pause 4s]
And now, the gentlest part.
You're going to look for three good things in this day. Just three.
They don't need to be big. Often the best ones are tiny.
A patch of sunlight on the pavement. A message that made you smile. A song on the radio. The first coffee, nice and hot.
Take your time. Let whatever comes, come, without hunting for the best answer.
Here's your first good thing. It doesn't matter what it is.
See it again for a moment. Where were you? What could you see, what could you hear?
And notice how it feels, right now, to think back on it. Maybe a little warmth in your chest. The start of a smile.
Savour it, like a square of chocolate you let melt slowly on your tongue.
We often walk straight past these small moments. The brain is built to remember what went wrong. So tonight, you show it the rest as well.
[pause 4s]
Now, a second good thing.
Maybe something someone did for you. Or something you did for someone else.
Or simply a moment when you felt at home in yourself, even for a minute.
Go over the details. A colour, a smell, the sound of a voice, the temperature of the air.
Keep it close. Let it take up a little room, a few seconds longer than usual.
If a smile comes, let it form. If nothing stirs, that's fine too. Simply thinking back on it already counts.
[pause 3s]
And a third.
If nothing comes, that's alright. The good thing can be this one: you're lying here, warm, taking care of yourself.
That's already a lot.
Or maybe something small arrives. A taste, a bit of light, a quiet moment between two tasks. Welcome it.
Rest your attention on it, the way you'd rest your hand on a warm mug, just to feel the heat.
Your three good things are here, resting gently beside you, like three small lights.
No need to hold on to them. They've already changed the colour of this day, just a little.
Before you close the book, one last gesture.
Say thank you. To yourself, quite simply.
Thank you for getting through today. Thank you for what you did, and even for what you tried.
You can say it in your own words, silently. Softly, the way you'd say it to a tired friend.
Thank you to your legs, for carrying you all day. Thank you to your hands, for all they did. Thank you to your mind, which thought so hard, and can finally rest.
You did your best with what you had today. And tonight, that's enough.
If your nights stay difficult week after week, do talk to a health professional about it.
[pause 4s]
Now the page is turned.
Your body can grow heavy. First your feet, sinking into the mattress.
Then your calves. Your knees. Your thighs, heavy and warm under the duvet.
Your hips settle. Your lower back spreads out. Your belly rises and falls, all on its own.
Your shoulders sink. Your arms slide down along your sides. Your hands are loose, open, soft.
The back of your neck lets go. Your jaw unclenches. Your forehead smooths out.
Your eyelids are heavy, so very heavy.
Your breath slows, without any help from you.
In… and out… like a very slow wave on the shore.
The warmth of the duvet. The quiet of the room.
Nothing left to do. Nothing left to tidy away.
You can drift, very gently, toward sleep.
The day is put away…
and the night begins.

sessions.title: Count down to sleep
script: Tonight, we're going to count. Not sheep: breaths.
From fifty down to one, one number on each out-breath.
It's a very simple task, almost boring. And that's exactly what a mind needs when it still wants to work.
We give it a small job. Enough to keep it busy. Not enough to wake it up.
A bit like handing a rattle to a child who isn't ready to sleep yet. They hold it, they look at it, and without noticing, their eyes begin to close.
Before we start, settle in for the night.
Lie down in the position you usually fall asleep in. Pull the duvet up to wherever you like it. Find the hollow in the pillow, the one that already knows the shape of your head.
Let your arms rest wherever they're comfortable. If anything bothers you, a crease in the sheet, a strand of hair, a leg at an awkward angle, take a moment to sort it out now.
After that, you won't need to move. The bed will take care of everything else.
[pause 3s]
One rule, just one: if you lose count, it doesn't matter at all.
If you can't remember whether you were on thirty-two or twenty-eight, pick whichever number you like and carry on from there.
If your breath doesn't line up with my voice, that doesn't matter either. Your breath is right. Follow it, and let my voice trail along behind, like a quiet background sound.
And if you fall asleep before the end, that's perfect. As the subtitle says, few people make it to the end.
It isn't a contest. Nobody's checking. There's no right way to count, only yours.
To begin, three breaths, a little slower than usual.
Breathe in gently through your nose, feeling the cool air coming in…
[pause 3s]
and let the air flow out for a long time, warm now, through your nose or your mouth.
Again. Breathe in, feeling your belly rise under the duvet…
and breathe out, feeling it fall, very softly, like a balloon slowly emptying.
One last time. Breathe in…
[pause 3s]
and breathe out, letting the full weight of your body drop into the mattress.
Now let your breath return to its natural rhythm. Stop steering it. It knows what to do. It does this every night without you.
On each out-breath, I'll say a number. You can repeat it in your head along with me, like an echo.
And between the numbers, I'll invite you to let go of one small part of your body.
Here we go.
Fifty. The air leaves, and your shoulders drop a little, away from your ears.
Forty-nine. Your forehead smooths out, like a sheet pressed flat by hand. The space between your eyebrows grows wider.
Forty-eight. Your jaw loosens. Your teeth part. Your tongue rests, soft and heavy, at the bottom of your mouth.
Forty-seven. Your hands open, very gently, fingers slightly apart. There's nothing left for them to hold.
Forty-six. The back of your neck settles into the pillow, and the pillow takes the whole weight of your head.
Forty-five. Your chest softens. It doesn't need to hold itself up anymore. It barely rises at all.
Forty-four. Your belly is soft. It rises and falls by itself, like a slow wave rolling up the sand.
Forty-three. Your back spreads out on the mattress, one vertebra at a time, from the top all the way down.
Forty-two. Your hips sink a little deeper. Your thighs grow heavy, warm and still.
Forty-one. Your calves, your ankles, your feet let go, down at the bottom of the bed. Even your toes are resting now.
Forty. Your whole body is resting. From head to toe, there's nothing left to carry.
[pause 4s]
Now we'll leave a little more space.
I'll only say every other number. The one in between, you count on your own, on the next out-breath.
Meanwhile, my voice will stay here, very low, telling you gentle things. You can listen to it, or let it drift past.
No need to be precise. If you skip a number, or count the same one twice, let it be. The numbers are there to carry you, not to keep an eye on you.
Thirty-nine.
On the next breath, you'll count thirty-eight on your own. Or maybe you won't. It makes no difference at all.
Thirty-seven. Imagine each number is a step, and you're walking down a staircase covered in thick, soft carpet.
Your feet make no sound. The handrail is smooth and warm under your hand. You go down without hurrying, one step for each breath.
Thirty-five. With each step it gets a little darker, a little softer, a little warmer.
As if you were heading down to a room where someone has already switched on a small lamp and drawn the curtains. The bed is made. The sheets are cool and clean.
Thirty-three. Your body is as heavy as a sack of sand set down on the floor. Once it's down, it doesn't move. It simply takes the shape of whatever is beneath it.
Thirty-one. Your head sinks into the pillow, like into a drift of fresh snow. Silent. Soft. All around you, the world goes quiet.
Twenty-nine. If thoughts pass by, let them pass. They can make noise in the distance, like a street behind a closed window. You only have one number to hold, nothing more.
Twenty-seven. Your eyelids are heavy. They rest like two little curtains drawn for the night. Behind them, everything is dark and gentle.
Twenty-five.
Halfway. Notice how much slower your breath is than at the start. You did nothing to make that happen. It slowed down by itself, number by number.
From here, you carry on by yourself.
My voice will only give you a few landmarks now and then. In between, count at your own pace, each time the air leaves.
If you drift off track, pick up anywhere. The number doesn't matter. What matters is the breath going down, and you going down with it.
As you count, imagine a smooth stone sinking slowly to the bottom of a lake. It drifts down, silently, through calm, warm water.
It has nothing to do to sink. It simply lets itself be carried downward, further and further from the surface.
Up there are the day, the noise, the screens. Down here, there's only light slowly fading, layer after layer, from pale blue to deep blue.
Your body is like that stone. Heavy, smooth, still.
You sink with each breath, a little deeper into the mattress.
At the bottom of the lake there's fine sand, and the stone settles into it without a sound. It has arrived. It can stay there all night long.
[pause 4s]
Twenty, more or less. Or somewhere else. It doesn't matter.
Your arms are so heavy you could forget where they are. They feel warm, as if they were resting in a patch of sunlight.
Your legs too. They melt into the sheets, as if they were part of the bed.
And that heaviness rises slowly, from your feet to your knees, from your knees to your belly, from your belly to your chest. A quiet warmth, taking all the time it needs.
Now picture a tall building in the evening. Every window is lit.
And one by one, floor by floor, the lights go out. Gently. In no particular order.
Each window that goes dark is a thought going to bed.
The office on the third floor. The kitchen on the fifth. A bedroom right at the top. The building grows dark and quiet, just like you.
[pause 4s]
Fifteen, perhaps.
The numbers are getting blurry. They're spreading out. Some of them disappear.
That's normal. In fact, it's a sign you're drifting.
If you're still counting, count more slowly. If you've stopped, there's no need to start again.
Outside, perhaps, a few snowflakes are falling through the night. They land on rooftops, on cars, on branches. Without a sound. Each in its turn.
Think of an hourglass. The sand falls, grain by grain. At the bottom it forms a small, soft, motionless heap.
Your breath is like that sand. It flows, slowly, and it settles.
Twelve, or thirteen. Your breathing has become so light you can barely feel it, just a small coming and going at the edge of your nostrils.
Your jaw is loose. Your cheeks are loose. Your whole face has softened, like the face of someone already asleep.
Your hands lie heavy and warm on the sheet. You couldn't quite say where your fingers end and the fabric begins.
The next number can come. Or not. Your breath simply carries on, patient and steady, without you having to look after it.
There's nothing left to hold on to. Not the numbers, not the day, not tomorrow.
Just the breath, coming in… and going out.
If your nights are often difficult, consider talking to a health professional one day. For now, let the numbers carry you.
Ten…
Your shoulders are heavy. Your hands are heavy.
Your head is resting. Your whole back is resting.
[pause 4s]
Heavy… warm… slow…
The bed holds you. The night wraps around you.
Nothing to do… nothing to hold…
Keep counting… or let it all go…
[pause 5s]

sessions.title: Unwind before sleep
script: Good evening. It's time to set the day down.
There's nothing special you need to do for these few minutes. Just listen, and let yourself be guided towards the night.
Settle into bed in whatever position suits you best tonight. On your back, arms by your sides. Or on your side, one knee slightly bent.
Take a moment to move a little, if your body wants to. Stretch your legs. Wiggle your toes. Turn your head gently to one side, then the other.
Then find the place where everything stops. The hollow waiting for you in the mattress, warm and familiar.
You can close your eyes now. Or leave them half-closed, if you prefer, your gaze resting nowhere in particular.
Simply notice what's here. The room. The darkness, or the dimmed light. The temperature of the air on your face, a little cooler on your nose and cheeks.
The weight of the duvet, resting over you like a calm, steady hand. The pillow under your cheek or the back of your neck.
[pause 4s]
The day was whatever it was. Long, perhaps. Full. Or just ordinary.
To help you leave it behind, here's an image you can borrow for a moment.
Imagine your day is a room, somewhere in your home.
A room with the light still on, a bit untidy, with all the day's things lying around.
The emails. The conversations. The to-do list. The noise of the commute. The small annoyances. The questions that still have no answer.
You're standing in the doorway. You look at the room one last time, without needing to tidy anything.
Everything in there will stay there. Nothing will get lost. Tomorrow, if you need it, you'll know exactly where to find it.
Now reach for the light switch. And turn off the light.
The room goes dark. The day's things fade into shadow, one by one, like furniture under dust sheets.
Then, gently, you pull the door towards you.
It closes. You hear the soft click of the latch.
[pause 4s]
On this side of the door, there's only the night. The quiet. Your bed.
You have nothing left to carry until tomorrow. No more meetings, no more messages, no more answers to give.
If something from the day comes knocking on the door, that's alright. You hear it, you notice it. And you leave it on the other side.
Now, come to your breath.
Just notice the air coming in and the air going out, without changing it for now.
Maybe it's still a little quick, a little high in your chest. That's completely normal at the end of a day.
If you like, rest one hand on your belly, just below the navel. The other can stay where it is.
Under your hand, feel your belly rise as the air comes in, and fall as it leaves. Gently. Like a small boat on calm water.
Now let the out-breath grow longer. Just the out-breath.
No need to count. Instead, imagine the air leaving like a balloon slowly letting itself down, without being squeezed.
You breathe in normally… and let the air out for longer, all the way to the end, unhurried.
[pause 4s]
An out-breath that's longer than the in-breath can help the body slow down. It's a very simple signal, a way of telling it the day is over.
The air comes in, cool… and flows out, warm, like a long, silent sigh.
Once more. The air comes in without effort… and leaves slowly, taking a little of the day's tiredness with it.
And at the end of each out-breath, there's sometimes a tiny moment of stillness. A small dip, before the next breath arrives by itself.
You don't need to make it happen. Just notice it, when it's there.
It's a little like the quiet between two waves, when you're lying by the sea. You don't wait for it. It comes, and it goes.
If at any point you feel short of air, return straight away to your natural breath. Nothing should be forced.
[pause 4s]
Keep this slow breath in the background. And while it carries on, we'll relax the body, starting with the face.
Your forehead first. Let it widen, as if someone were gently smoothing a thumb between your eyebrows.
Your eyes, behind your eyelids. They have nothing left to look at. They can rest deep in their sockets, heavy and still.
Your eyelids themselves grow heavy, like two small velvet curtains drawn for the night.
Your cheeks. Your mouth. Let your lips barely touch.
Your jaw, above all. That's often where the day hides. Let it loosen, teeth slightly apart.
Your tongue can come away from the roof of your mouth and rest, soft and heavy, at the bottom.
And all around your ears, your temples, your scalp, let a softness spread, like warm water flowing slowly over your head.
Your shoulders, now.
All day long, they've been carrying. A bag, a screen, responsibilities, other people's worries.
Tonight, they can come down. On an out-breath, let them slide towards the mattress, a little lower. Then a little more.
Notice the space opening between your shoulders and your ears. The back of your neck lengthens. Your throat softens.
If there's still a knot somewhere, between your shoulder blades or at the base of your neck, don't try to undo it. Just send your breath its way, and let it melt in its own time.
Your arms follow. Your elbows. Your forearms. Your wrists.
And your hands. Let them open, palms up or palms down, whichever they like.
Notice your fingers one by one. Thumb. Index finger. Middle finger. Ring finger. Little finger.
They have nothing left to hold, nothing to type, nothing to scroll. Only to rest.
You might feel a gentle warmth in your palms, or a faint tingling in your fingertips. Let it simply be there.
Your chest, now. It rises and falls without any help from you. Let it open a little, like a window left ajar on a quiet night.
Your belly becomes soft, round and loose. It doesn't need to hold itself in anymore. It can spread out freely under the duvet.
[pause 4s]
Now feel your whole body lying on the bed.
Feel the places where it touches the mattress. The back of your head. Your shoulder blades. Your lower back. Your heels.
With each out-breath, you sink a little deeper. As if the mattress were becoming deeper, softer, more welcoming.
You don't have to hold yourself up. The bed is holding you.
Your back can spread out. Your hips can grow heavy. Your legs can grow heavy, all the way down to your feet.
Your thighs sink into the sheet. Your knees let go. Your calves become soft and heavy.
Your ankles relax, and your feet fall slightly to the side, however they like.
Imagine sinking into warm sand in the evening sun. The sand moulds itself to every curve of your body.
It's warm under your calves, under your thighs, under your back. It holds you everywhere at once, and you have no effort left to make.
You might notice how different your body feels from a few minutes ago. Heavier. Wider. Slower. Or maybe not yet, and that's fine too.
[pause 4s]
Nothing left to do. Nothing left to decide.
Now let your breath return to its natural rhythm. You don't need to lengthen it anymore. It has found its own pace.
It comes and goes on its own, like the tide rising and falling on the beach.
You can simply watch it from a distance, the way you might watch waves without counting them.
Each breath a little slower than the last. Or maybe not. It doesn't matter. There's nothing left to check.
You drift gently, from one breath to the next, like a leaf floating down a quiet river, carried along by the current.
Listen, too, to the sounds of the night around you. Rain, perhaps. A car passing in the distance. The quiet of the house.
All these sounds belong to the night. They ask nothing of you. They might even rock you to sleep.
The rain falls on the roof, drop after drop, steady and soft. Each drop arrives, and then it's gone.
If thoughts pass by, let them pass. They're on the other side of the door.
You don't have to chase them away. They can wait until tomorrow, safely tucked away in that dark room.
If your sleep troubles go on for a while, a health professional can support you. Tonight, you can simply rest.
My voice will grow quieter now, and soon it will fade away. You can let it go, and stay right here, in the warmth of your bed.
The door is closed. The room is quiet.
Your body is heavy… and warm…
Your shoulders are resting. Your hands are resting.
The breath comes… and goes…
Soft… slow… still…
Everything slows down…
The bed holds you. The night is here.
Goodnight.
[pause 5s]

sessions.title: Cognitive shuffle
script: Tonight, we're going to play a little game. A very quiet game, played with your eyes closed, lying in bed.
First, settle in as if you were going to sleep. Turn onto whichever side you like. Let your head find its place in the pillow.
Pull the covers up to wherever feels right. Let your arms rest wherever they want to, without arranging them.
If your mind is reasoning tonight, arguing, planning tomorrow, this game is for you.
As we fall asleep, our thoughts change shape. They come loose. An image of a cat, then a staircase, then a colour, with no link between them.
Some researchers think we can imitate that moment. By picturing random objects, unrelated to one another, we give the brain the impression that sleep is already on its way.
And above all, we keep it just busy enough to let go of its ruminating. It's hard to replay an argument while you're picturing a giraffe.
The rule is simple. I'll give you a word. We'll take it one letter at a time.
For each letter, I'll suggest a few objects beginning with that letter. You picture one for a few seconds, then move on to the next.
You don't need to see them clearly. A blurry image is enough. Even just the idea of an image is enough.
This isn't a memory test, or an imagination contest. If an object doesn't come, move on to the next one. If a different object turns up instead, take it. It'll do just fine.
And above all, don't try to connect them. No story, no logic, no reason. An apple, then a piano. That's all there is to it.
Before we start, two easy breaths.
Breathe in through your nose, without forcing…
[pause 3s]
and breathe out gently, letting your body sink a little further into the mattress.
[pause 4s]
Once more. The air comes in, cool in your nostrils… and flows out, a little warmer, a little slower.
Then let your breath find its own rhythm again. You don't need to look after it any more.
The first word is BEACH. B, E, A, C, H.
We'll start with the letter B.
A balloon. A red balloon, its string trailing, floating against a white ceiling. See the light shining on its round surface.
A bicycle. An old blue bicycle leaning against a garden wall. A few drops of rain still resting on the saddle.
A button. A big wooden coat button, with four little holes in the middle.
A bowl of cherries. Dark red, shiny, stalks sticking up every which way. A small white napkin folded beside it.
A loaf of bread. The crust golden and crackly, a dusting of flour on top. Maybe its warm smell, fresh from the oven.
A boat. A narrowboat moored on a canal, pots of geraniums on the roof, a bicycle propped against the cabin.
A butterfly. Its wings slowly opening and closing on a warm stone wall.
A blanket. A thick wool blanket, folded over the arm of a sofa, its fringe a little tangled.
A bucket. A red plastic bucket, upside down on the sand, a little spade lying next to it.
If a thought from the day slips in between two objects, that's fine. Let it be, and come back to the letter. Always the letter.
The letter E.
An egg. A brown egg in an egg cup, a tiny feather stuck to the shell. A slice of buttered toast waiting on the plate beside it.
An envelope. A brown paper envelope, no address, lying on a desk by a window.
An eraser. A white eraser, worn down at one corner, with a few grey crumbs around it.
An elephant. An old grey elephant, standing quite still, flapping just one ear.
An easel. A wooden easel in an empty room, a blank canvas resting on it, a brush on the ledge.
An elm leaf. Yellow, a little curled, lying on a park bench after the rain.
An earring. A single silver earring, forgotten on a bedside table, catching a little light.
An eiderdown. Big and puffy, spilling over the side of an old bed.
[pause 4s]
The letter A.
An apple. A green apple on a wooden table, smooth and cool under your hand.
An anchor. A big rusty anchor lying on a quay, a coil of thick rope next to it, gulls standing about.
An apricot. Orange, slightly fuzzy, still warm from the sun.
An accordion. Folded, silent, in its case lined with red velvet.
An armchair. A deep, faded armchair by a window, a cushion squashed in one corner.
An acorn. A small acorn with its little cap, resting in the palm of a hand.
An aquarium. One small orange fish turning slow circles, bubbles rising one by one to the surface.
An attic. Dusty and quiet, a single beam of light falling across the wooden floor.
You might notice your mind hopping from one object to the next. That's exactly what we're after. There's no right answer.
The letter C.
A cat. A ginger cat curled up on a windowsill, its tail wrapped around its nose. Its side rising and falling, very slowly.
A candle. A white candle, the flame standing straight, a drop of wax sliding slowly down the side.
A cup. A blue china cup, a spoon resting on the saucer.
A cloud. A single white cloud, alone in a pale sky, changing shape so slowly you can hardly tell.
A carrot. Fresh from the ground, a little soil still clinging to it, its leafy top bright green.
A cello. Propped in a corner, one string slightly loose.
A cushion. Round and velvet, a deep green, with a small dent where someone's head has been.
A cardigan. Grey, soft, hung on the back of a kitchen chair, the sleeves dangling.
If a letter gets you stuck, skip it. There's no penalty, nothing to get right.
[pause 4s]
The letter H.
A hat. A straw hat hanging on a hook by the back door.
A hammock. Strung between two apple trees, swaying ever so slightly, a book left open in the bottom.
A hedgehog. A small hedgehog snuffling through fallen leaves at dusk, its tiny black nose twitching.
A honey jar. Golden, a wooden dipper resting inside, a slow thread of honey falling back down.
A harp. Tall and still, in the corner of a quiet room.
A hot-water bottle. Wrapped in a knitted cover, warm against your hands.
A haystack. Golden in a field at the end of the day, a few loose strands lifting in the breeze.
That's the end of the word. You don't need to remember anything you saw. It's already fading, like the images of a dream on waking.
The balloon, the elephant, the cat… They can go back to wherever they came from.
Just notice whether your body is a little heavier. Whether your breath is a little slower. Whether the thoughts from earlier feel a little further away.
[pause 4s]
Let's take a second word. This time, we'll go more slowly. Fewer words, more space between the images.
The word is SOFT. S, O, F, T.
The letter S.
A sock. A thick wool sock, drying on the radiator, its heel a different colour.
A seashell. A pale pink shell, ridged and smooth, lying on wet sand.
A saucer. A white saucer, a teaspoon on top, a few grains of sugar left behind.
A snowman. Slightly lopsided, a scarf around his neck, alone in a quiet garden. His carrot nose points a little towards the sky.
A sailing boat. Small and white, far out on a calm sea.
A slipper. A sheepskin slipper, warm inside, waiting by the side of a bed.
A sofa. Deep and worn, the cushions sagging just where you would sit.
[pause 4s]
The letter O.
An orange. Round, its peel slightly bumpy under your fingers. Maybe its scent, as your thumb sinks in to peel it.
An owl. Perched on a branch, perfectly still, its eyes half closed. Its feathers puffed up against the cool night air.
An oar. A wooden oar resting across a rowing boat tied to a jetty.
An olive. A single green olive in a little earthenware dish.
An oven glove. Checked red and white, hanging from a hook.
An onion. Golden, its skin as thin as paper, crackling a little under your thumb.
An otter. Floating on its back on a still river, its paws folded on its chest.
The letter F.
A feather. A white feather drifting slowly down through the air, swaying from side to side, landing without a sound.
A fern. Its fronds uncurling in a shady corner of a garden.
A fig. Purple, soft, split open a little at the top, showing the pink inside.
A fence. A low wooden fence, its paint peeling, a cat walking slowly along the top.
A fireplace. Embers glowing low, a log settling with a soft crackle, the warmth reaching your feet.
[pause 4s]
The letter T.
A teapot. A round brown teapot, a wisp of steam rising from its spout.
A tulip. A single yellow tulip, very upright, in a narrow vase.
A towel. A thick white towel, folded on the end of a bed, still warm from the dryer.
A teddy bear. Sitting alone on a shelf, one ear coming unstitched, looking slightly to one side.
A tortoise. Moving across a lawn so slowly, its shell warm from the afternoon.
From now on, you can carry on by yourself.
Pick a word of your own, a gentle word with nothing worrying about it. GARDEN. PILLOW. CHERRY. Whatever comes.
Take its first letter. Let an object come. Then another. Then another.
For example, with the letter G. A goldfish in a round bowl. A pair of gloves on a bench. A guitar against a wall. A gate at the end of a lane.
Then the letter A. An almond. An apron hanging on a hook. An apple tree in blossom, petals falling on the grass.
Take your time with each one. A few seconds. Long enough to see it, even vaguely. Then let it go, without regret, and take another.
When you run out of ideas, move to the next letter. And if you forget the word, make up a new one. It doesn't matter at all.
If your nights stay restless for a long time, think about speaking to a health professional. Tonight, just let the images come.
[pause 4s]
A letter… an object…
then another…
no link… no effort…
a blurry image… drifting away…
and your body, carried… very gently…
[pause 5s]

sessions.title: Quiet a racing mind
script: It's busy up there tonight. Ideas follow one another, answer each other, circle back. And sleep is struggling to find a way in.
You haven't done anything wrong. A mind that races at bedtime is often a mind that hasn't had a minute to itself all day. It's making the most of the quiet.
During the day there's noise, screens, other people. At night, in the dark, there's only the mind left. So it unpacks everything.
So we won't ask it to be quiet. That never really works. The more you chase a thought away, the faster it comes running back.
We'll do something else. Let the thoughts be there, and learn not to follow them.
It's a skill, like any other. It's learned gently, night after night. And tonight, you don't need to master it. Just try it, a little.
Settle in first. On your back, or on your side, whichever you prefer.
If your eyes want to close, let them. If they'd rather stay half open in the dark, that's fine too.
Take a breath a little fuller than the others… and let it go without holding on.
[pause 4s]
One more. Fill up gently… and empty out completely, like a long, slow sigh.
Then let your breath find its own rhythm again. You don't need to guide it any more.
To begin, we'll give your attention somewhere to land. Not in your head. Lower down. In your body.
Feel the weight of your body on the bed.
Your head, first. It's heavy in the pillow. You can feel the exact place where it rests. The back of your skull, your temple, or your cheek.
Your neck, with nothing left to hold up. The small muscles around your jaw, which can loosen a little, your teeth slightly apart.
Your shoulders. Your upper back. Notice how supported they are, without you having to do a thing.
Your arms, lying by your sides or on the covers. They're growing a little heavier, a little softer. Your hands, open or half closed, however they like.
Your pelvis, often the heaviest part. It sinks a little deeper than the rest, settling into its own small hollow in the mattress.
The backs of your thighs. Your calves. Your heels. All of it is resting. All of it is held.
And your feet, right at the end. Maybe a little coolness on your toes, or instead a soft warmth, tucked in under the duvet.
[pause 4s]
This weight is your anchor for tonight. It's always there. It doesn't think, it doesn't plan. It simply weighs.
And this bed will still be holding you in an hour, and at dawn. There's nothing you need to hold up yourself.
Each time you get lost in your thoughts, you can come back here. To the weight of your body on the bed.
Of course, thoughts will come. That's guaranteed. And that's fine. They'll be our practice.
When a thought arrives, give it a little name. A label, a single word, said silently, in a calm inner voice.
Not to analyse it. Just to recognise it. A bit like saying "oh, a bus" when a bus goes by in the street.
A few labels come up often.
If you're thinking about tomorrow, what you need to do, which order to do it in, you can say: planning.
If you're replaying a scene from the day, a conversation, a face, you can say: remembering.
If you're wondering what will happen, whether it'll go well, what you'd do if it went wrong, you can say: worrying.
There are others, if you like. Judging, when a small voice comments on what you did or didn't do. Rehearsing, when you're scripting a conversation that hasn't happened yet.
And if you're not sure, the word "thinking" works perfectly well. There's no wrong label.
Let's try it together. Let whatever comes, come. Don't go looking for anything in particular.
When a thought appears, name it. Planning. Remembering. Worrying. Thinking.
Then come back to the weight of your body on the bed.
For example, you think: I must call the garage tomorrow before ten. You notice, and you name it: planning. Then you feel your pelvis, heavy on the mattress.
Or you see your colleague's face in that meeting again. Remembering. And you come back to your heels, resting at the bottom of the bed.
Or a small voice tells you that you should have answered differently. Judging. And you feel your shoulders, broad and quiet against the sheet.
And maybe, all of a sudden, you find yourself preparing exactly what you'll say to someone tomorrow, word for word. Rehearsing. And you come back to your hands, resting, still.
That's all. A thought, a word, the body. And then again, as many times as you need.
[pause 4s]
Maybe the same thought comes back three times in a row. You name it three times. That isn't failing, that's the practice.
Maybe you were lost for a long while before you noticed anything. That's normal too. The moment you notice is the moment that counts.
What happens when you name a thought is a small step to the side. You're no longer inside it. You're looking at it.
It's still there, but it's a little less sticky. A little further away.
A bit like the difference between standing in the rain and watching the rain from behind a window. Same rain. But you're dry, and warm, and you can let it fall.
To help you find that distance, imagine you're lying in a bedroom beside a country road, at night.
Every so often, a car passes in the distance. You hear its engine approaching, and maybe you see the headlights sweep slowly across the ceiling.
Then the sound fades. The light disappears. The room is dark and quiet again.
A little later, another one. A truck perhaps, heavier, slower. Then a scooter, high-pitched, in a hurry. Then nothing for a long while, just the hush of the countryside and the room around you.
You don't know where they're going. You don't need to know. They aren't your journeys.
Your thoughts are like those cars.
They arrive, they pass, they move on. You don't need to stop them. You don't need to get in.
You stay in your bed, warm and heavy. You hear them go by, far off, on the road, and you let them keep going.
[pause 4s]
Sometimes a car slows down. A thought insists, honks its horn a little.
You can give it its label. Worrying. Planning. And let it continue on its way.
It has its own destination. You stay here, warm, under the duvet, with nowhere you need to be until morning.
And if you notice you've climbed into the car, that you're already driving off with it towards tomorrow or yesterday… just step out.
Without blaming yourself for anything. Come back to your room. To your bed. To this body, heavy and quiet.
Now, come and feel the points of contact.
The sheet under your hands. Its texture. A little smooth, or a little rough. Cooler in some places, warmer where your skin has been resting for a while.
The pillow against your face or the back of your neck. Its softness. Its warmth, right where your head lies.
The duvet over your feet and legs. The slight weight of it. Like a wide, light hand resting on you.
Maybe the air is a little cooler on the tip of your nose, or on your forehead. And under the covers, a gentle warmth, settling in.
These sensations don't talk. They don't plan anything, and they don't replay anything either. They're simply here, now, keeping you company.
If you like, move one finger very slightly across the sheet. Feel the fabric glide under your fingertip. Then let your hand go still again, heavy, resting.
It's a very simple anchor, one you can return to at any moment of the night, even if you wake up later on.
[pause 4s]
When a thought comes, name it. And come back to the sheet. To the pillow.
A car goes by… its lights slide across the ceiling… and the room is quiet and dark again.
Now we'll add something very small.
On each out-breath, let the air leave a little more slowly. Just a little. As if you were blowing on a cup of herbal tea that's too hot.
The in-breath stays natural. Only the out-breath stretches, without forcing.
If at any point it feels uncomfortable, or you're short of air, simply return to your usual breathing.
The air comes in… and goes out, taking its time.
[pause 4s]
With each out-breath, your body weighs a little more on the bed.
On one out-breath, your shoulders. On the next, your arms. Then your belly, rising and falling all on its own. Then your legs.
As if each breath leaving set a little more of you down into the mattress.
A quiet warmth, perhaps, in your hands. In your belly. Or nowhere in particular. Either is perfectly fine.
Thoughts may still be passing. Further away. Less often. Or not.
You don't have to count them. You don't have to do better than last night.
Maybe you'll simply notice that the cars are passing less often. That the road is quieter. That the silences between them are growing longer.
And in those silences, there's you, lying here, heavy, still.
You don't need to fall asleep. Sleep will come when it's ready, in its own time, like the tide that always finds its way softly back up the sand. You're resting, and that's already plenty.
[pause 4s]
I'll speak less and less now. You know what to do, and it's very little.
A thought comes. A word. And back to the weight of the body.
If you've drifted off somewhere, no problem. The bed is still here. So is your weight.
A word, if a thought passes. Then the sheet under your hand.
Planning… and your pelvis, heavy.
Remembering… and your head, in the hollow of the pillow.
Worrying… and the breath flowing out, slowly, all by itself.
The out-breath, a little longer, a little softer.
Your shoulders sinking. Your legs, heavy. Your hands, warm.
The warmth under the covers, wrapping around you a little more with every breath.
If night-time overthinking has been spoiling your nights for a long time, a health professional can help. Tonight, you've already done a lot.
[pause 4s]
A car, far away…
then the quiet.
The road, completely silent, under a moonless sky.
The weight of the body… the sheet… the breath…
Nothing to do… nothing to hold on to…
[pause 4s]

sessions.title: Heavy body, quiet mind
script: Tonight, your body may still be holding on to the day. Stiff shoulders, a clenched jaw, legs that won't keep still.
For these fifteen minutes, I'd like to offer you two very old, very simple sensations: heaviness, and warmth.
It's a method that's been around for nearly a century. It's called autogenic training. The idea fits in one sentence: you silently repeat short phrases, and let your body respond in its own time.
Why heaviness and warmth? Because they're the natural sensations of a body letting go. When muscles release, your arms and legs feel heavier.
And when the body relaxes, blood flows more freely to the hands and feet, and they slowly warm up.
By thinking of these sensations, you walk that path in reverse. You invite your body to take the shape of rest.
You don't have to make anything happen. You say the words in your head and notice what follows. Sometimes a lot.
Sometimes almost nothing. Both are fine.
Lie on your back, if that's comfortable for you. Arms by your sides, a little away from your body, palms however they like.
Legs stretched out, slightly apart, feet falling naturally outwards.
If your back pulls, you can slide a cushion under your knees. If you prefer sleeping on your side, stay on your side. The phrases work there too.
Take a moment to move one last time. A small stretch, a yawn if one wants to come, a little adjustment of the pillow under your neck.
After that, the idea is to stay still. Not rigid. Just resting, like a leaf that has landed on water.
Let your eyes close. Breathe normally. Don't try to breathe better.
Just feel the air coming in and going out, at its own pace. A little cooler as it comes in through your nose, a little warmer as it leaves.
Notice the places where you're supported, too. The back of your head in the pillow.
Your shoulder blades on the mattress. Your hips, your calves, your heels.
Everywhere your body touches the bed, there's support. And everywhere there's support, you can let a little more weight settle down.
[pause 3s]
You can begin with the core phrase. The one that opens and accompanies everything else.
Repeat silently, slowly, leaving a space after each word: I am… completely… calm.
I am completely calm.
Don't ask yourself whether it's true. It isn't an order, and it isn't a lie.
It's a direction. Like pointing someone the way.
You can have a thousand things on your mind and still say: I am calm. The words open a door. The rest will follow, or not, tonight or another night.
I am calm. Let the words settle, like a pebble drifting slowly down to the bottom of a pond, and resting there.
If your mind wanders, towards tomorrow, towards a conversation, towards a list of things to do, that's completely normal. Come back to the phrase, without hurrying.
I am completely calm. Say it once more, more slowly, the way you'd say goodnight to someone you love.
[pause 3s]
Now, heaviness.
Start with your right arm. If your left side feels more natural, you can start there instead, whichever feels right to you.
Bring your attention to that arm. The shoulder. The upper arm.
The elbow. The forearm. The wrist.
The hand, right to the fingertips.
Feel how it rests on the mattress. Its weight.
The place where it touches the sheet. The fabric under your skin, cool or already warm.
And silently repeat: my right arm is heavy.
My right arm is very heavy.
Imagine it filled with warm sand, flowing slowly from the shoulder down into the hand. The sand gathers in your palm, in your fingers, and the hand grows weighty and still.
Or imagine it's become so heavy that lifting it would take real effort. You don't need to try. Just imagine it.
My right arm is heavy, so heavy.
Like the arm of a child asleep in the back seat of a car. Completely limp. If someone lifted it, it would simply flop back down.
Notice whatever sensations arise. A tingling, a numbness, a feeling of sinking.
Or nothing in particular. All of it is right.
The elbow opens a little. The wrist softens. The fingers curl gently, all by themselves, like the fingers of a sleeping hand.
My right arm is heavy. And I am calm.
[pause 3s]
Now, the left arm. The shoulder, the upper arm, the elbow, the forearm, the wrist, the hand.
My left arm is heavy.
My left arm is very heavy. It sinks into the mattress, like a damp piece of clothing laid on the bed, following every fold of the sheet.
Feel the weight of the hand most of all. The back of the hand, or the palm, pressing into the sheet. The fingers spreading a little, on their own.
And the shoulder easing backwards, as if it were opening. It doesn't need to stay ready anymore. It can rest now.
My left arm is heavy, heavy and peaceful.
Both my arms are heavy. Heavy and resting.
They have nothing left to carry, nothing left to hold. No bag, no phone, no steering wheel, no worries.
Maybe one arm responds more than the other. That's very common.
The body isn't symmetrical, and it doesn't have to be. Let each side go at its own pace.
I am calm. My arms are heavy.
[pause 3s]
Now the heaviness moves down into your legs.
The right leg first. The hip, the thigh, the knee, the calf, the ankle, the foot.
My right leg is heavy.
My right leg is very heavy. Like a log lying in the grass. It doesn't move anymore.
Feel the thigh spreading out, the back of the knee drawing closer to the mattress, the heel making a small hollow in the bed.
The foot tips gently outwards. The ankle loosens. Even the toes can rest now.
My right leg is heavy, from the hip all the way down to the heel.
Now the left leg. From the hip all the way to the toes.
My left leg is heavy.
My left leg is very heavy. The heel sinks, the calf spreads, the thigh becomes weighty and soft.
Like after a long walk in the mountains, when you finally lie down and your legs feel as if they're made of lead. A good kind of tiredness. A tiredness that has earned its rest.
All day, your legs have carried you, up stairs, down streets, from room to room. Tonight, it's the bed that carries them.
My legs are heavy. My arms and legs are heavy.
Take a moment to feel all four limbs at once. Four quiet weights, resting on the bed, all around you.
And notice, perhaps, that the middle of your body has softened a little too. Your back spreading wider. Your pelvis heavier.
As if the heaviness of your limbs had spread to everything else, little by little, the way water slowly soaks into a sponge.
I am completely calm.
[pause 4s]
Now, to this heaviness, you can add some warmth.
Not a strong heat. A gentle warmth, like a lukewarm bath, or an autumn sunbeam resting on your skin.
Come back to the right arm. Feel the skin of your hand, the inside of your elbow, the soft hollow of your wrist.
My right arm is warm.
My right arm is very warm. Imagine slowly lowering it into water at just the right temperature. The warmth rises from your fingertips up to your shoulder.
Or imagine sitting on a terrace late in the afternoon, with the sun resting on your forearm. You feel the skin growing warm, little by little.
Maybe your fingers tingle a bit. Maybe your palm feels thicker, fuller. That's relaxation finding its way through you.
My left arm is warm.
My left arm is very warm. Your hand may feel a little fuller, a little more alive. Like slipping on woollen gloves on a cold winter morning.
The warmth glides along the forearm, wraps around the elbow, rises to the shoulder, and settles there, like a cat curled up in a ball.
My arms are warm. Heavy and warm.
[pause 4s]
The warmth flows down into your legs.
My right leg is warm.
My right leg is very warm. As if a soft blanket had just been laid over it, a blanket that had been left for a while in front of the fireplace.
The warmth wraps around the thigh, the knee, the calf. It moves through the ankle and down into the foot.
My left leg is warm.
My left leg is very warm. Right down into the foot, right down into the toes.
Cold feet are often what keeps us from falling asleep. Let the warmth settle there, gently, without forcing anything.
Imagine a hot water bottle at the bottom of the bed, resting against the soles of your feet. The warmth spreads into your heels, into your arches, in between your toes.
My arms and legs are heavy and warm.
Heavy, as if they were sinking into the mattress. Warm, as if they were wrapped in soft wool. Let those two sensations blend together.
I am completely calm.
[pause 4s]
Now, come to your belly.
Rest a hand on it if you like, just above your navel. Otherwise, simply bring your attention to that place.
Imagine a small source of warmth deep in your belly. Like a cup of herbal tea held in your hands, but on the inside.
My belly is warm. A gentle warmth glows deep in my belly.
My belly is very warm. The warmth slowly spreads, towards your ribs, towards your lower back, towards your hips.
That's often where the knots of the day like to hide, deep in the belly. Let the warmth surround them, without trying to undo them. They may loosen all on their own.
Your belly softens. It doesn't need to stay pulled in. It can round out and let go, like bread dough quietly rising somewhere warm.
My belly is warm, and my whole body softens around it.
[pause 4s]
And your breath, all this time?
You don't need to do anything with it. It carries on by itself, as it has since the start of the evening, since the start of your life.
The phrase is: it breathes me.
It breathes me. As if you were being carried by the breath, instead of steering it.
Your belly rises, and falls. Like a small boat on a very calm sea, lifting and sinking with the swell.
My breathing is calm and even. It breathes me.
You don't have to lengthen it, or slow it down. It knows exactly what your body needs. You can trust it, the way you'd trust the current of a slow, peaceful river.
Maybe you notice a tiny pause, right at the bottom of the out-breath. A moment where nothing moves, before the air returns.
There's nothing to do with that moment. Just let it be there.
If you feel dizzy or uncomfortable at any point, set the phrases aside and simply return to your natural breathing.
It breathes me, quietly, all on its own.
[pause 4s]
Before moving to your face, feel your shoulders and the back of your neck. The warmth from your arms may have risen up there too.
Your shoulders round and settle, as if they'd been wrapped in a woollen shawl. Your neck lengthens on the pillow. Your head grows heavy, and the pillow receives it.
And now, your face.
Your whole body is heavy and warm. But your forehead can stay cool. Like stepping out onto a balcony on a summer evening, when a light breeze brushes across your face.
My forehead is pleasantly cool.
My forehead is cool. A cool forehead, a clear, light head, resting on the pillow.
Let your eyebrows soften too. Your eyelids grow heavy. Your jaw loosen, teeth slightly apart, tongue resting.
Your cheeks soften. Your lips barely touch. The tiny muscles around your eyes, the ones that have looked at screens all day, can finally rest.
Your whole face is relaxed. Forehead cool.
Cheeks soft. Mouth at peace.
[pause 4s]
Now, gather it all together. Let the phrases melt into one another, slowly, like colours spreading through water.
My arms and legs are heavy and warm.
My belly is warm.
It breathes me.
My forehead is cool.
I am completely calm.
Feel your whole body, heavy and warm, resting on the bed. Like a stone still holding the warmth of the evening sun.
The mattress holds all of you. You have nothing left to hold up. Not your arms, not your legs, not your head, not the day.
Go through it all, without hurrying. Your arms, heavy and warm. Your legs, heavy and warm.
Your belly, gently warm. Your breath, coming and going on its own. Your forehead, cool.
And everywhere, this calm settling in, like snow covering a garden during the night, without a sound.
If the words fade, let them fade. The sensations can carry on without them.
If anything bothers you, warmth that feels too strong, a heaviness that feels unpleasant, simply drop the phrase and come back to your natural breathing.
Tonight, there's nothing to come back to. No waking up, no getting ready. You can stay exactly as you are, and let sleep arrive whenever it wants.
If your body stays tense night after night, or if you've been sleeping badly for a long time, it's worth talking to a health professional.
[pause 4s]
Your body is heavy. It sinks, a little further, into the softness of the bed.
It's warm. A quiet warmth, from your shoulders all the way to your feet.
Your breath comes and goes. On its own. Like the sea, far away.
You are calm.
Heavy…
warm…
calm…
[pause 5s]
It breathes you…

sessions.title: Bedtime body scan
script: For the next twenty minutes, you have only one thing to do: lie still, and listen.
We'll travel through your whole body, slowly, very slowly, from your feet to the top of your head.
And in each place, we'll switch it off. The way you switch off the lights in a house at night, room by room, before going to bed.
Why does this help? Because attention can't be everywhere at once. While it wanders slowly through your body, it's no longer circling around tomorrow.
And a body that's looked at with kindness tends to let go all by itself.
It's very likely you'll fall asleep before the end. In fact, that's the plan. If it happens, let my voice carry on without you. It doesn't need you to listen.
[pause 3s]
Lie on your back if you can. It's the simplest position for a body scan.
But if you fall asleep more easily on your side, choose your side. Your sleep comes before the method.
Let your arms rest by your sides, or your hands on your belly.
Legs stretched out, slightly apart. Feet falling loosely, each to its own side.
Take a moment for any last adjustments. Pull the duvet up to your chin, if you like. Plump the pillow. Brush a strand of hair from your face.
Shift your shoulders a little so they find their place. Gently roll your head to the right, to the left, then back to the centre.
Look for the position where nothing pulls and nothing pinches. The one you could stay in for hours.
And when everything is in place, let yourself become still.
If something itches or bothers you later on, you're allowed to move. Scratch, adjust, then come back to stillness. This isn't a test.
Listen for a moment to the sounds around you. The rain outside, perhaps. A car somewhere far off. The soft hum of something in the house.
There's nothing you need to do with them. They can stay there in the background, like a rug of sound for you to rest on.
Close your eyes, if they aren't closed already.
And begin by listening to your breath, without changing it.
Notice where you feel it most. Maybe at the edge of your nostrils, slightly cool air coming in, slightly warmer air going out. Maybe in your chest. Maybe in your belly.
There's no right place. Just choose the one where the breath feels easiest to follow.
Now let that breath slow down a little.
Breathe in easily, without puffing up your chest. Just what you need.
[pause 3s]
And breathe out for a little longer. As if the air were taking the stairs instead of the lift. Step by step, in no hurry at all.
[pause 4s]
Once more. The air comes in, without effort, like a wave sliding gently up the sand…
and flows out, slowly, all the way to the end, like the wave drawing back.
[pause 3s]
With each out-breath, your body grows a little heavier. A little more settled.
You don't need to count. You don't need to get it right. Your breath will find its night-time rhythm on its own.
If at any point you feel short of air, simply return to natural breathing.
Notice the small pause right at the bottom of the out-breath. That very quiet moment when the air has left, and nothing is rushing in yet.
You can rest in that hollow. Just for a moment. Then the in-breath returns by itself, without you having to reach for it.
[pause 3s]
Now we'll begin the journey. Right at the bottom. With the feet.
Bring your attention to your right foot.
Start with the big toe. Feel its shape, its nail, its weight. The touch of the sheet or the duvet, right at the tip.
Then the second toe, next to it. The third, a little smaller. The fourth. And finally the little toe, right at the edge of the foot.
Maybe you can feel them clearly. Maybe you can hardly feel anything. Both are normal. It's enough just to rest your attention there, like a light hand.
Feel the tiny spaces between your toes. The air, or the warmth, tucked in there.
Feel the sole of the foot. The padded part just below the toes, which has carried you with every step today.
The curve of the arch, softer, touching nothing at all.
The heel, round and firm, resting on the mattress, carrying the whole weight of the leg.
Feel the top of the foot, where the duvet rests. The fine little bones under the skin. And the ankle, round and bony.
Now imagine a small light glowing in that foot. A night-light, soft and golden.
And gently, as you breathe out, that light dims. It fades. Then it goes out.
The right foot is switched off. It has nothing left to do tonight. It rests in the dark, peaceful.
Maybe it feels heavier than the other. Or warmer. Or different, in a way that's hard to describe. Just notice, without trying to understand.
[pause 3s]
The left foot, now.
The big toe first. Its weight, its warmth. Then the second toe. The third. The fourth. The tiny one, at the edge.
Let each toe loosen, drifting just slightly away from its neighbour, like children falling asleep side by side.
The sole of the left foot. The arch, light, suspended. The heel, well settled, sinking ever so slightly into the bed.
The top of the foot, under the light weight of the covers. The left ankle.
Here too, a small light. Let it dim… gently… until it goes out.
The left foot is switched off.
[pause 3s]
Both feet are resting in the dark now. Heavy. Warm. Still.
All day long, they've carried you. Along pavements, up stairs, down corridors. Tonight, they have nothing left to carry.
Imagine them sunk into fine sand, still warm from a summer's day. The sand covers your toes, your heels, your ankles, and holds the warmth around them.
A slow warmth that doesn't move. That wraps around. That makes your feet so heavy they seem to become part of the sand.
Moving up to the calves.
Feel your right calf. Its roundness. Its weight on the mattress. The muscle inside, which can loosen like a rope being slackened.
Feel the shin, at the front, just under the skin. And the back of the leg, softer, spreading a little across the sheet.
Let the calf become soft, like dough left to rest somewhere warm.
And on the out-breath, let the light in the right calf go out too.
The left calf. Its weight. Its warmth. The muscle unwinding, fibre by fibre.
The shin, at the front. The back of the leg, growing a little heavier with every breath.
And the light dimming… dimming… and going out.
You may know this feeling, after a long walk, when you finally sit down and your legs grow heavy, almost numb. Let that good heaviness come.
[pause 3s]
Your feet, your ankles, your calves. Your whole lower legs are switched off.
Notice how far away this part of your body feels now. Blurrier. Like a shore you leave behind by boat, fading into the mist.
The knees, now.
Feel your right knee. The front, the kneecap, under the duvet. The back of the knee, that soft little hollow that may be touching the mattress.
Let that hollow soften. Let the knee grow heavy.
And the light in the right knee goes out.
The left knee. The kneecap. The hollow behind. Everything that bends and straightens all day, and tonight can stay still.
How many times did these knees bend today? To sit down, to stand up, to climb a step, to pick something up. They can rest now.
The light dims… and goes out.
The thighs.
These are big muscles, often tense without our noticing. Feel your right thigh. Its length. Its weight, spreading across the bed.
Feel the front of the thigh, under the duvet. The inner side, more tender. The back, resting along its whole length on the mattress.
Let it grow heavier still. As if it were sinking a little into the mattress.
The light in the right thigh goes out.
The left thigh. Heavy. Broad. Let go.
Feel the skin of your thigh against the sheet. The fabric slightly cool on one side, the warmth of the duvet on the other.
Let this big muscle unfold and soften, like a wool jumper laid over a chair at the end of the day.
It too switches off.
And now, the pelvis.
Feel your hips. The hip bones, on either side. Your buttocks, carrying a large part of your weight.
Feel your lower belly, below the navel. The inside of the pelvis, like a wide bowl.
Let all of it settle. Sink down into the mattress, like sand drifting to the bottom of the water.
The pelvis is the body's centre of gravity. When it lets go, everything else often follows. The legs widen. The lower back spreads. The belly softens.
And the light in the pelvis dims, slowly… and goes out.
[pause 3s]
The whole lower half of your body is switched off now. From your toes to your hips.
It's dark and soft down there. All is calm. Nothing moves.
If you got lost along the way, if you're thinking about something else, that's fine. Just come back to wherever my voice is.
The mind wanders, that's its nature. A shopping list, a conversation, a song. Each time you notice, bring it back, without scolding. The way you'd call back a puppy that's wandered off the path.
And if you feel sleep arriving, if your thoughts turn strange or drift apart, let them. It's often a sign that the night is already carrying you off.
Moving up to the belly.
Feel your belly rising as the air comes in, and falling as it goes out.
It doesn't need to be flat, or held in. It can be round, soft, relaxed. Let it be exactly as it is.
Feel your navel, and the space around it. The hollow under your ribs. The sides of your waist, sinking a little into the bed.
You might imagine a small warmth in the middle of your belly, like a hot-water bottle resting on it. It spreads gently, out to the sides, round to your back.
A round, patient warmth. Like a mug of herbal tea held between your hands.
And on an out-breath, the light in the belly dims… and goes out.
[pause 3s]
The back, now.
Start with the lower back. That curve just above the pelvis, which may be touching the mattress, or may not.
Let it spread. Lengthen. As if each vertebra were moving ever so slightly away from the next.
The middle of the back. The ribs, at the back, moving gently with the breath.
The upper back. The shoulder blades, lying flat on the bed, like two folded wings.
Your whole spine, from bottom to top, resting on the mattress. Supported. Held. You don't need to hold yourself up anymore.
If you feel a tighter spot, somewhere between your shoulder blades or in your lower back, send your out-breath there. Imagine the air reaching it, and warming it a little.
The light in your back goes out. Vertebra by vertebra. Like lamps along a long corridor being switched off one by one, starting from the far end.
[pause 3s]
And the chest.
Feel your chest rising and falling, gently, under the duvet.
Feel your ribs, like a supple cage opening and closing.
Maybe you can feel your heart beating, somewhere in there. You don't need to do anything with it. It does its work quietly, as it does every night.
Let your chest soften. Widen a little.
We often keep the chest a little closed, a little guarded, without realising. Tonight, you're safe. It can open, just slightly, like a window left ajar to the night.
And the light in the chest dims… and goes out.
Your belly, your back, your chest. Your whole torso is switched off.
Only a few rooms in the house are still lit. We'll go there gently.
The hands.
Feel your right hand. The thumb first. Its fleshy base, its nail, its tip.
The index finger. The middle finger, the longest. The ring finger. And the little finger, right at the edge.
Let each finger uncurl just a little, open up, and stop holding on to anything.
The palm. The hollow of the hand, warm and soft. The back of the hand. The wrist.
These hands have done so much today. Held, carried, typed, opened, closed. Tonight, they can open and hold nothing at all.
Maybe you can feel something in your fingertips. A faint tingling, a pulse, some warmth. That's life flowing quietly, all the way to the edges.
The light in the right hand goes out.
The left hand. Thumb. Index finger. Middle finger. Ring finger. Little finger.
The palm, the back of the hand, the wrist.
Let it become heavy and limp. Like an empty glove lying on a table.
And the light in the left hand goes out.
The arms.
The forearms first. Feel their weight on the mattress, or on your belly.
The elbows, a little pointed, leaning into the bed. The upper arms, up to the shoulders.
Let them grow so heavy you could forget they're there.
Like heavy branches laden with snow, no longer trying to lift. They bow. They settle.
The light in both arms dims… and goes out.
And the shoulders.
The shoulders are often the attic of the day. We pile everything up there. Responsibilities, tension, things we mustn't forget.
Tonight, you can clear out the attic.
No need to sort. No need to tidy it all. You just open the skylight and let the night air in.
Let your shoulders drop, away from your ears. Let them widen, flatten onto the mattress.
Feel the tops of your shoulders, that little ledge where we carry bags and worries. Let it melt, like butter spreading slowly in a warm pan.
And on a long out-breath, the light in your shoulders goes out.
[pause 3s]
Only the head is left. The last room with the light on.
Start with the back of your neck, resting on the pillow.
Let your head weigh its full weight. The pillow takes all of it. You don't need to hold it up anymore.
Feel the front of your neck too. The throat. The place where you swallow. Let it soften, open, as if a collar that was too tight had just been undone.
The light in your neck goes out.
The jaw.
Feel where it hinges, just in front of your ears.
Let your teeth part a little. Let your tongue rest on the floor of your mouth, soft and wide.
Let your lips barely touch.
The whole lower face grows heavy, easy, a little slack. Like just before a yawn.
The light in your jaw goes out.
Your ears, now. They've heard so much today. Voices, engines, notifications, slamming doors.
Tonight, they don't need to stay on guard. The sounds of the night can reach them, or not. They're resting.
Your cheeks, growing round and heavy. Your nose. The air brushing the edge of your nostrils.
Your eyes, now. Feel your eyelids resting on your eyes, like two petals.
Behind your eyelids, your eyes can rest. They have nothing left to look at. No screen, no face, no road.
Let them sink back gently, heavy and still.
The light in your eyes goes out.
[pause 3s]
And the forehead.
Feel the whole surface of your forehead. Your eyebrows. The space between them, where worries sometimes settle.
Let your forehead smooth out. Widen. Like the surface of a lake when the wind has dropped.
Your temples. The top of your head. The back of your head.
Imagine all the skin of your scalp relaxing, like after a head massage at the hairdresser's. A fine, light ease, flowing slowly down to the back of your neck.
And very gently, the last light in the house dims… dims a little more… and goes out.
[pause 3s]
Now all the lights are out.
Your body is no longer made of separate parts. No more feet, legs, arms on their own.
There is just one quiet mass, heavy and warm, resting in the dark.
Like a hill under snow, at night. Still. Silent. Peaceful.
Perhaps you can no longer quite tell where your hands end and the sheets begin. Where your feet stop. That's normal. That's the body falling asleep.
Let this quiet mass spread out, melt into the mattress, into the warmth of the duvet, into the darkness of the room.
The breath carries on by itself, inside this quiet mass. Rising… falling…
Like the sea, far away, beyond the dunes. You can't see it. You can barely hear it. But it's there, steady, and it never stops.
You have nothing to do. Nothing to watch over. The house is asleep.
And if a thought still drifts by, it passes far away. Like a car's headlights gliding across the ceiling, then gone.
You don't need to follow it. It leaves on its own, and the dark comes back, soft and deep.
Feel the warmth that has settled everywhere. In your feet, in your legs, in your belly, in your hands.
An even, quiet warmth, like a bed you've already been sleeping in for hours.
Feel the weight, too. That good, heavy weight holding you against the mattress. You couldn't fall.
The mattress holds you. The duvet covers you. The night keeps watch over the house.
There's no time anymore. No list. Nothing to get ready.
Only the breath, slow… and the warmth… and the dark.
[pause 3s]
If you've been finding it hard to sleep for a long time, it may help to talk to a health professional. For now, just rest.
Heavy… and warm…
Each breath carries you a little further.
Further… deeper… softer.
[pause 3s]
Everything is switched off…
[pause 5s]
everything is still…
[pause 5s]
the night can begin…

sessions.title: The lighthouse keeper
script: Settle in comfortably, in the position you like to fall asleep in. Pull up the duvet, and let your head sink into the pillow.
Tonight, I'm going to tell you a story. A very simple story, where almost nothing happens.
You don't need to follow it to the end. You don't need to remember any of it.
If your attention drifts away, let it go. If you fall asleep in the middle, that's just as it should be.
Simply let my voice keep you company, like the sound of the sea heard from far off, through an open window.
[pause 4s]
It's the end of a September day, on the coast of Brittany.
The sky is clear. It rained a little in the morning, and now the air is rinsed clean, very bright, with that smell of salt and seaweed you only find by the ocean.
On the slipway of the little harbour, a man is waiting, a canvas bag at his feet. His name is Loïc. He's a lighthouse keeper.
Tonight, he's going back to his island, for a week on watch.
The ferryman arrives in his boat, an old wooden launch painted blue, the paint flaking a little at the edges. The engine makes a steady, reassuring sound. Put, put, put.
The two men greet each other with a nod. They've known each other a long time. They don't need to say much.
Loïc steps aboard. He sits at the back, his bag between his knees, and the boat slips gently out of the harbour.
The sea is calm. Just a long, lazy swell that lifts the boat, lets it down, and lifts it again.
The wooden bench is warm beneath him, heated by the afternoon sun. Through the soles of his boots, he can feel the slow, steady hum of the engine.
Behind them, the village grows smaller. White houses with blue shutters, the grey church tower, small boats resting on the sand at low tide. Everything becomes small, then distant, then blurred.
